comments.author: 015UUZn8aEvW
comments.text:
One of the takeaways from this, and from the 2023 OpenAI saga, is that a firm's nominal governance structure isn't necessarily its real governance structure.
Note that I'm not making any judgement about whether Huang or Altman
should
have been fired. The point is that in both cases, the board members were nominally empowered to make that decision, and did make it, rightly or wrongly. But when the rubber hit the road, it turned out that there were other forces that overruled them.

stories.title_en: GLM-5.4: Toward generalized coding with our first loop transformer

comments.author: HarHarVeryFunny
comments.text:
I love the transparency, or at least given technical details, that Zhipu provide - a refreshing change from the locked-down approach of the western companies, and an interesting glimpse into the direction of SOTA LLMs.
Looped Transformers are an obvious direction even if there are still problems to be worked out. The original Transformer is a bit like an unrolled for loop, and rather unnaturally pairs different sets of weights, both for attention and feed forward (knowledge) with different "layers" (aka loop iterations). Far more natural is to strive for something more like our brain's thalamo-cortical loop and association cortex, where "thought" is iterative and there are no restrictions as to what patterns/knowledge get applied when.
A similar idea has been explored before ("Universal Transformer", 2019), seemingly going nowhere, but perhaps "necessity is the mother of invention" and compute-starved Chinese companies are finding a way to make it work.

comments.author: aurareturn
comments.text:
For those wondering what loop transformers are:
LLMs have layers of data, called weights. During inference, each layer gets computed once. Moving weights from HBM memory to the chip is a major bottleneck because to generate a token, you need to move an entire layer into the chip, compute once, move it out, move the next layer in. Hence, memory bandwidth has been the #1 bottleneck for inference.
A loop transformer optimizes this bottleneck. Instead of one layer being computed once, it will compute the same layer multiple times, increasing the model intelligence without relying memory bandwidth as much. Bandwidth is still important, but not as much anymore.
More intelligence is squeezed by using the GPU compute that is typically sitting idle during inference.

stories.title_en: What does it mean to understand what we built?

comments.author: sandinmyjoints
comments.text:
I have been doing some research on different kinds of understanding.
Language learning has notions of receptive vs. productive knowledge. Receptive knowledge lets someone read or listen and understand. Productive knowledge lets them speak or write. Learners can typically understand far more than they can produce.
Memory psychology has recognition vs. recall. Recognition means identifying the right answer when it's in front of you, as on a multiple-choice test. Recall means producing it from nothing. Recognition is consistently easier.
Some sociologists have what they call interactional vs. contributory expertise. Interactional expertise is the ability to talk fluently about a field, follow its debates, and judge work plausibly. Contributory expertise is the ability to actually do the work.
There's no question that as I use AI more, I move from the former category to the latter category when it comes to coding. The thing I'm trying to prevent with AI usage is making that same move with the whole system. But is prompting sufficient as the mechanism of production / recall / actually doing the work?

comments.text:
>However, Lattimore’s highly idiosyncratic conceptualisations invert reality. comments.author: bryanlarsen
comments.text:
Lootable food stores is what made the state.
States developed in areas which developed lootable food stores:  wheat, rice, corn, smoked salmon, et cetera.
Areas which developed agriculture which was not lootable did not develop states.   For instance the parts of the world that relied on potatoes, cassava, taro and yams did not develop states.   The best way to store those is in the ground, so they can't be stolen at scale.
The first kings were bandit kings, and we had city-states long before horses and transport.
States larger than the city state required transport.
The first cities like Jericho and Çatalhöyük predate any dates in the article by several thousand years.  River based civilizations like Egypt and Uruk were a couple of thousands of years after Jericho.
ref: _Against the Grain_, James C. Scott
